results.title: It's Not about Race: Good Wars, Bad Wars, and the Origins of Kant's Anti-Colonialism
Colonialism in Kant’s Political Philosophy
Kant and Slavery—Or Why He Never Became a Racial Egalitarian
results.abstract: Abstract:According to an oft-repeated narrative, while Kant maintained racist views through the 1780s, he changed his mind in the 1790s. Pauline Kleingeld introduced this narrative based on passages from Kant’s Metaphysics of Morals (1797) and “Toward Perpetual Peace” (1795). On her reading, Kant categorically condemned chattel slavery (and colonialism) in those texts, which meant that he became more racially egalitarian. But the passages involving slavery, once contextualized, either do not concern modern, race-based chattel slavery or at best suggest that Kant mentioned it as a cautionary tale for labor practices in Europe. Overall, Kant never explicitly considered chattel slavery as a moral problem to be addressed on its own. Rather, he treated it primarily in terms of its function in human history. If he ended up expressing some qualms about its practices, it was likely because they threatened to deepen intra-European conflicts and undermine the prospect of perpetual peace. The humanity of the enslaved “Negroes” was never part of the reasoning. This was not a casual oversight on Kant’s part. It reflects the complexity of his philosophical system: everything he did or did not say about chattel slavery begins to make sense once we connect his philosophy of history and his depiction of “Negroes” as natural slaves.

results.abstract: Kant’s Nonideal Theory of Politics is a very welcome addition to the growing roster of recent studies of Kant’s politics. Unlike many, which concentrate on a particular policy area (such as colonialism or just war theory), Huseyinzadegan’s aim is a systematic one: namely, to sketch out a hitherto underspecified ‘non-ideal’ political realm to complement the ideal theory for which Kant is best known. Her most original claims centre on what she calls ‘political Zweckmässigkeit’, for on her account, the main rules that are to guide the political actor in non-ideal circumstances are the regulative teleological principles elaborated in the first and third Critiques, as well as occasional writings, including, most famously, the Idea for a Universal History, What is it to Orient Oneself in Thinking, and Perpetual Peace. By linking political action in a non-ideal world with such familiar critical principles she hopes not only to situate such action within Kant’s larger critical framework, but also to provide a ready means of disassociating Kantianism rightly understood fromhis less savoury positions on gender, race and Eurocentric history. Huseyinzadegan especially associates such unfortunate tendencies of Kant’s thought with his embrace of a Eurocentric ‘cosmopolitanism’, which she sharply distinguishes from ‘peace’, as the object of ideal politics. Unlike ‘peace’, cosmopolitanism in a political, as distinguished from strictly moral, sense is, on her reading, a revisable regulative ideal that guides Kant’s own non-ideal politics as it stands, but that is also deeply compromised by Eurocentrism and naïve assumptions as to the benignity of ‘commerce’. The aim of her effort is not only to salvage what is worth keeping in Kant’s ideal theory but also to open a path toward a revised version of non-ideal politics (not offered in Huseyinzadegan’s current study) in which the goals of Kant’s ideal theory might be pursued through regulative principles that were both more respectful of human diversity and fallibility and more mindful of both the dark side of commerce and the ongoing burden BOOK REVIEWS

M. A. R. Habib. Hegel and Empire: From Postcolonialism to Globalism. London: Palgrave Macmillan, 2017. ISBN: 978-3-319-68411-6 (hbk). 164 pp. £49.99.
results.abstract: As the discipline of philosophy begins to come to terms with its entanglements in histories of colonialism, Eurocentrism and white supremacy, there is an increasing demand for scholarship that rigorously interrogates what these histories mean for the practice of philosophy today. WithHegel and Empire,M. A. R. Habib asks some of the important questions that emerge in this regard, in so far as they relate to Hegel’s philosophy and the legacy of Hegelian dialectics. In this sense it is, on paper, a welcome contribution to a growing literature which uses insights from critical race, postand de-colonial studies to rewrite the history of philosophy. However, and unfortunately, the book also represents a missed opportunity for a relevant intervention into this academic field since it fails to construct a compelling account of the possible relations between Hegel’s philosophy, the conceptions of empire and imperialism which we might find therein, and the realities and consequences of modern imperial domination and colonial exploitation. This could be excused if the primary purpose was to act as an introductory volume on Hegel and Eurocentrism and as a guide to further readings within post-Hegelian literature on this topic. Such is indeed the format indicated by the outline of the book since chapters which contain readings of Hegel’s writings (first and foremost the master–slave dialectic but also passages from the the lectures on the philosophy of world history, art and religion, including the infamous loose manuscript sheets on the geographic base of historical determinations) are paired with short summary chapters which delineate select responses from what might broadly be described as a ‘critical tradition’. What the strategy of fusing readings succeeds with, is to introduce the central and decisive question concerning the degree to which Eurocentrism can be conceived of as engrained within Hegel’s philosophy as a whole. The reader gets an introduction to (a) Susan BuckMorss’s and Andrew Cole’s respective ‘historical’ interpretations of the master– slave dialectic (in Buck-Morss’s Hegel, Haiti and Universal History 2009 and Cole’s The Birth of Theory (2014)), (b) Frantz Fanon’s Black Skin, White Masks (1952), and (c) Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s commentary on Hegel’s engagement with the Bhagavad Gita (from A Critique of Postcolonial Reason, 1999). results.title: Kritik der phänomenologischen Vision
Othering Otherness - Stephen Muecke's Fictocriticism and the Cosmopolitan Vision
Editorial
Jean-François Lyotard
Susan Neiman, Left Is Not Woke
Response to Inés Valdez’s Review of Injustice and the Reproduction of History: Structural Inequalities, Gender and Redress
results.abstract: Cosmopolitanism—the view that all human beings, independent of their national affiliations, are of equal concern and, thus, that justice applies to the cosmos— may seem a radical theoretical and political project, especially in our current times characterized by the worldwide upsurge of nationalistic and antiglobal feelings. In her incredibly powerful and ingenious work, Inés Valdez shows that, to unleash the emancipatory potential of cosmopolitanism, we need to move beyond existing and influential neo-Kantian understandings of cosmopolitan justice. Valdez masterfully demonstrates that such accounts are ultimately ill equipped to (1) theorize the transnational nature of injustice (i.e., the intrinsically intertwined oppression of marginalized subjects within and outside the “West”); (2) recognize the necessity of political spaces that not only “exceed the domestic and international spheres” (p. 7) but also unravel and denounce their racialized and imperial foundations; and (3) center the cosmopolitan project not on “the charitable Westerner” but on “subaltern colonized and neocolonized subjects” and their political struggles (pp. 7–8). In so doing, Valdez’s book is a major contribution to international political theory, the history of international political thought, critical race theory, and international relations. Valdez advances an account of “transnational cosmopolitanism” that is normatively compelling and original, as well as methodologically creative. Normatively, it overcomes the weakness of neo-Kantian cosmopolitan proposals and offers an invaluable framework to theorize and assess our postcolonial cosmos marked by “unequal sovereignty, racialized labor exploitation, and neoliberal capitalism” (p. 14). Methodologically, her account is developed by innovatively juxtaposing a “disloyal” reading of Kant’s (and neo-Kantian) principles of “complementarity” between different realms of politics and of “hospitality”withW. E. B. Du Bois’s post–WorldWar I writings on the global “color line” and his political activism. After starting with a brand-new contextual interpretation of Kant’s Toward Perpetual Peace, which questions the usefulness of his critique of colonialism to an emancipatory cosmopolitanism (chapter 1), Valdez scrutinizes whether the “hierarchical strands of [the Kantian] framework may resurface in [those contemporary] approaches indebted to it” (p. 56) by insightfully engaging with neo-Kantian cosmopolitans (chapter 2). Valdez argues that, despite their well-meaning intentions, neo-Kantian cosmopolitans fail to grapple with transnationalism and are still affected by Eurocentrism in that they (1) take the European federal institutional project as the model to be expanded to the whole world, (2) overlook “anti-colonialism as a political practice and intellectual tradition” (p. 57), or (3) neglect the imperial origins of international projects like the League of Nations and the European Union. For Valdez, transnationalism can be fully theorized only when Kant’s principles of “complementarity” and “hospitality” are transfigured through looking at the intellectual and political work of marginalized subjects who mobilized against the transnational nature of racial domination and crafted “transnational alliances to contest . . . exclusion built around racial lines” (p. 86) in domestic politics and internationally. Chapters 3–5 develop a transnational cosmopolitanism by building on Du Bois’s thought and political mobilization as a cofounder and representative of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), as editor and writer of its magazine The Crisis, and as a crucial voice in the pan-African movement. The notion of “transnational cosmopolitanism” is distinctive in many respects. First, it reconceives justice and oppression as intrinsically transnational by identifying “the common threads of injustice behind slavery, colonialism, and neocolonialism” (p. 89) and “the shared experience of injustice” (p. 149) tying together racialized subjects across the world. Second and importantly, unlike other cosmopolitan projects that either reject the normative potential of identity or narrowly and problematically focus on national identity as a source of cosmopolitan commitments, transnational cosmopolitanism is nourished by specific and transformative identity-based forms of solidarity.
